120: Two responses to God's word sit side by side in this episode. In Jeremiah 36, King Jehoiakim hears the scroll read aloud, cuts it apart and burns it piece by piece. No one in the room is afraid. In Joel 2, the Lord calls his people to do the opposite: to return to him with all their heart, tearing their hearts and not just their clothes, because he is gracious, merciful and slow to anger. The difference is trust. One man will not let God's word tell him the truth. The other invitation assumes God can be believed, even when what he says is hard. That is why we sang 'Tis So Sweet to Trust in Jesus and Undivided Heart. Trusting Jesus means taking him at his word and asking for a heart that is not split between him and everything else.
122: This episode is about the blood of Jesus and what it says. Hebrews 12:24 calls him the mediator of a new covenant, whose sprinkled blood speaks a better word than the blood of Abel. Abel's blood cried out for justice. The blood of Jesus speaks forgiveness for the guilty. Second Corinthians 5:21 explains how that can be: the one who knew no sin was made to be sin for us, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God. The songs follow the same line. Isaiah 53 sings the prophecy of the servant who was pierced for our transgressions, and Jesus Thank You is the plain response of someone who knows what that cost. We come to God on the strength of what Christ has done, not what we have done.
123: Psalm 118 opens with a call and an answer. Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good. Then Israel, the house of Aaron and everyone who fears the Lord are each told to say the same thing back: his steadfast love endures forever. The repetition is the point. God's people need to say it to each other until they believe it. Psalm 73:25 turns that truth into a personal confession. The psalmist has looked at everything heaven and earth can offer and says there is nothing he desires besides God. We sang Forever and Some Come Through Fire in this episode. One celebrates a love that does not run out. The other remembers that God's people reach him by different roads, some of them hard, and that his love holds on every one of them.
125: This Friday Deep Dive is about the song Isaiah 53, which we recorded in 2011 with Sovereign Grace Music. Jonathan and Ryan talk through the story behind it and what the song means. The lyric stays close to the chapter it is named for. Isaiah 53 describes a servant who is despised and rejected, a man of sorrows who carries the griefs of others. He is pierced for our transgressions and crushed for our iniquities, and the punishment that falls on him brings us peace. Christians have always read the chapter as a portrait of Jesus at the cross, written centuries before it happened. The reading below is the chapter itself. Read it slowly before you watch, and the song will make more sense.
126: First John 1:8-10 does not let anyone off the hook. If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves. But the same passage gives one of the clearest promises in the Bible: if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness. Forgiveness rests on his character, not on how sorry we manage to feel. John 3:16-17 shows where that faithfulness comes from. God loved the world and gave his only Son, and he sent him to save the world, not to condemn it. We sang Depth of Mercy and Jesus Paid It All. The first asks whether there can really be mercy left for a sinner like me. The second answers it. The debt is paid, so confession is safe.
127: Paul tells the Corinthians what matters most, and he keeps it short. Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures. He was buried. He was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures. First Corinthians 15:3-4 calls this the message of first importance, the thing every other Christian truth depends on. Second Corinthians 5:21 says what the death accomplished: the sinless one was made sin for us, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God. The songs in this episode tell the same story from two angles. Flesh and Blood looks at the Son of God taking on a real human body in order to give it up for us. King of Kings follows the gospel from the manger to the empty tomb. Everything we sing starts here.
128: Isaiah called the coming servant a man of sorrows, and Peter says plainly who he is. First Peter 2:24-25 tells us Jesus himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, so that we might die to sin and live to righteousness. By his wounds we are healed. We were like sheep going astray, and now we have been brought back to the Shepherd and Overseer of our souls. First Timothy 2:5-6 adds that there is one God and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all. We sang Man of Sorrows and Undying Love. The sorrows he carried were ours. The love that carried them did not end at the cross, and it is why wandering people have somewhere to come home to.
129: This Friday Deep Dive tells the story behind Flesh and Blood, which West Coast Revival released in 2020. Jonathan and Ryan walk through how the song was written and its history. The title points to the center of the Christian faith: the Son of God became truly human. He did not appear to have a body. He had one, and he gave it up at the cross. Because he shared our flesh and blood, he can stand in our place and bring us to God. If you want to lead the song at your church after hearing how it came together, the free chord chart and the full lyrics are on the song page linked below.
130: Psalm 128 describes the ordinary blessings of a life lived in the fear of the Lord. You eat the fruit of your own work. Your family gathers around your table. You live to see your children's children, and there is peace on God's people. It is a picture of God's kindness in everyday things. Isaiah 42:3 shows the same kindness toward people who feel like they are barely holding on. The Lord's servant will not break a bruised reed or put out a faintly burning wick. Jesus is gentle with the weak. We sang Out of the Depths, a cry from someone who needs that gentleness, and Behold Our God, which lifts our eyes to the one who sits on the throne. The God who rules everything is the same God who is careful with us.
131: Romans 5:6-11 measures the love of God by its timing. Christ did not die for us after we cleaned ourselves up. While we were still weak, still sinners, still enemies, he died for the ungodly. Paul then argues from the greater to the lesser. If God reconciled us when we were his enemies, he will certainly save us now that we are his friends. So we rejoice in God through Jesus Christ. Jeremiah 31:3 says the same thing in a single line: the Lord has loved his people with an everlasting love, and he has kept being faithful to them. We sang I Could Sing of Your Love Forever and Before My Knees Could Reach the Ground. Both songs are about a love that was there first, before we did anything to ask for it.
132: Psalm 42 begins with thirst. As a deer pants for flowing streams, the psalmist's soul pants for the living God. He is not in a good place. His tears have been his food day and night, people keep asking him where his God is, and he remembers better days when he led the crowd to the house of God with glad shouts. The psalm gives words to believers who want God and cannot feel him near. First Corinthians 13:12 gives that longing a horizon. Now we see in a mirror dimly, but then face to face. The ache is real, and it will end. We sang As the Deer and Oh the Deep. The first is the prayer of the thirsty. The second looks down into the depth of God's love and finds there is no bottom to it.
133: Psalm 139:17 is a line of wonder. How precious are God's thoughts, and how vast is the sum of them. Philippians 2:5-11 tells us what those thoughts looked like in action. Christ Jesus, though he was in the form of God, did not cling to his rights. He emptied himself, took the form of a servant, and became obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross. Therefore God has highly exalted him and given him the name above every name, so that every knee will bow and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord. We sang O for a Thousand Tongues to Sing and The Wonders of Jesus Crucified. One voice is not enough to praise him, and the greatest wonder we have to sing about is the cross.
134: Psalm 122:1 is the song of someone who is glad to go to worship: I was glad when they said to me, let us go to the house of the Lord. Psalm 84:10-12 explains why. A single day in God's courts is better than a thousand anywhere else. The psalmist would rather stand at the door of God's house than live comfortably among the wicked. The Lord is a sun and a shield. He gives favor and honor, and he holds back no good thing from those who walk uprightly. We sang Better Is One Day and House of the Lord. Gathering with God's people is not a duty to get through. It is a gift, and a small taste of the day when we will be at home with him for good.
135: This Friday Deep Dive goes back to where The Wonders of Jesus Crucified came from. Jonathan and Ryan talk about the New Attitude conferences, about C.J. Mahaney, and about what it was like to write the song together for the church. It is a look at a particular season and at the people and preaching that shaped the songs that came out of it. The song itself does what its title says. It keeps the cross at the center and asks the singer to stop and wonder at it. If you have sung it for years, this episode fills in the story behind it. If it is new to you, start with the song, then come back and hear how it was written.
136: On the night before the cross, Jesus tells his disciples not to let their hearts be troubled. In John 14:1-6 he says he is going to prepare a place for them in his Father's house and will come back to take them to himself. When Thomas says they do not know the way, Jesus answers that he is the way, the truth and the life, and that no one comes to the Father except through him. In verses 12-14 he promises that those who believe in him will carry on his works, and that he will do whatever they ask in his name so the Father is glorified. We sang Abide and Completely Done. The work that makes us new is finished. What is left for us is to stay close to the one who finished it.
137: Second Corinthians 4:5-6 says what Christian ministry is about. We do not proclaim ourselves. We proclaim Jesus Christ as Lord. The God who said let light shine out of darkness has shone in our hearts, giving the light of the knowledge of his glory in the face of Jesus. Paul goes on to call that light a treasure carried in jars of clay, which gives this episode its title. The container is weak so that everyone can see the power belongs to God. Jude 24-25 ends on the same confidence. God is able to keep us from stumbling and to present us blameless before his glory with great joy. We sang Day After Day and All That Thrills My Soul. The treasure is Christ, and he is the one who keeps us.
138: Jesus teaches his disciples to pray with confidence in Luke 11:9-13. Ask, and it will be given. Seek, and you will find. Knock, and the door will be opened. He points to ordinary fathers, who know how to give good gifts to their children even though they are sinful, and says how much more the heavenly Father will give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him. Psalm 23:1-3 shows what that care looks like day to day. The Lord is my shepherd. He makes me lie down in green pastures, leads me beside still waters, and restores my soul. We sang Come Spirit of God and Renew My Life. Both are prayers, and both ask for what the Father has already said he is glad to give.
139: This Friday Deep Dive tells the story of All That Thrills My Soul, a hymn arrangement we released in 2013 with Sovereign Grace Music. Jonathan and Ryan talk through how the song came about. The heart of the hymn is in its title. Jesus is not one good thing among many. He is the one who satisfies, and everything else that thrills us is a gift from his hand. That is a hard thing to sing honestly, and it is why the song works as both a confession and a prayer. If you want to play it, the free chord chart is on the song page linked below.
142: Philippians 4:4 is a command, and Paul gives it twice: rejoice in the Lord always, and again I will say, rejoice. He wrote it from prison, which tells us this joy does not depend on how things are going. It depends on who the Lord is. Psalm 5:11 says the same thing. Let all who take refuge in God rejoice and sing for joy, because he spreads his protection over them. Joy and refuge go together. The people who are glad in God are the people who have run to him for safety. We sang Praise to the Lord and To Know You, Lord. The first calls everything that has breath to praise the King of creation. The second names the best reason for joy there is, which is knowing him.
143: Hebrews 11:1-3 defines faith as the assurance of things hoped for and the conviction of things not seen. By faith we understand that the universe was created by the word of God, so that what we see was not made out of visible things. Creation itself is the first lesson in trusting a God we cannot see. Psalm 27:13-14 applies that trust to hard days. The psalmist believes he will look on the goodness of the Lord in the land of the living, so he tells his own heart to wait, be strong and take courage. We sang All Creatures of Our God and King and Christ Is Mine Forevermore. Everything God made is called to praise him, and those who belong to Christ can wait for him with confidence.
144: Colossians 1:16 says that all things were created by Christ, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, and that all things were created through him and for him. The world is his in every sense. Ephesians 1:7-9 tells us what the Creator has done for the people who rebelled against him. In Christ we have redemption through his blood and the forgiveness of our sins, according to the riches of grace that God lavished on us. He has even made known to us the mystery of his will. We sang This Is My Father's World and Sooner Count the Stars. The first looks at creation and hears God in it. The second tries to count his mercies and gives up, because there are more of them than there are stars.
145: When Paul came to Corinth, he did not try to impress anyone. In 1 Corinthians 2:1-2 he says he decided to know nothing among them except Jesus Christ and him crucified. The cross was his whole message. Hebrews 12:1-2 tells us to run the race set before us the same way, with our eyes on Jesus. He is the founder and perfecter of our faith, and for the joy set before him he endured the cross, despised its shame, and sat down at the right hand of God. We sang The Old Rugged Cross and My Savior's Precious Blood. Both songs keep looking at the same place Paul did. The cross looked like defeat and shame, and it is where our forgiveness was won.
146: Jesus says something hard in Matthew 10:34-38. He did not come to bring easy peace. Following him can divide a household, and whoever loves father or mother, son or daughter more than him is not worthy of him. Whoever does not take up his cross and follow is not worthy of him. He asks for first place. In 1 Corinthians 2:2-5 Paul shows what that looks like in a messenger. He came in weakness and fear, preaching Christ crucified, so that faith would rest on the power of God and not on human wisdom. We sang And Can It Be and As Long As You Are Glorified. The first is amazed that the Savior would die for me. The second is the answer of someone who has put him first, whatever it costs.
147: The last chapter of the Bible shows where everything is headed. In Revelation 22, the river of the water of life flows from the throne of God and of the Lamb. The tree of life is there, and its leaves are for the healing of the nations. There is no more curse and no more night. God's servants will see his face. Three times Jesus says he is coming soon. Second Thessalonians 3:5 is a prayer for the meantime, that the Lord would direct our hearts to the love of God and to the steadfastness of Christ. We sang Oh to See You and There Is a Day. Both songs lean forward. The day is coming when faith becomes sight, and until then we ask for steady hearts.
148: Romans 12:1 is Paul's answer to the question of how to respond to God's mercy. Present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship. Worship is more than singing. It is your whole life handed over to him. Psalm 51:15 comes from David after his worst failure: O Lord, open my lips, and my mouth will declare your praise. Even the praise has to be given by God before we can give it back. We sang Plead for Me and Take My Life and Let It Be. The first leans on Christ, who speaks to the Father on our behalf. The second offers him our hands, our voices, our time and our will, one line at a time.
149: First John 1:5-10 starts with who God is. God is light, and in him there is no darkness at all. If we claim fellowship with him while walking in darkness, we are lying. But if we walk in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus cleanses us from all sin. Walking in the light does not mean having nothing to hide. It means we stop hiding, confess, and find him faithful to forgive. In 1 John 2:28-29, John tells us to abide in Christ so that we have confidence when he appears. We sang Inside Out and Here With Christ. God changes people from the heart outward, and the safest place to be honest about our sin is close to the one who died for it.
150: John 1:1-5 goes back before creation. In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. All things were made through him. In him was life, and the life was the light of men, and the darkness has not overcome it. Colossians 1:15-20 says the same about Christ in different words. He is the image of the invisible God. All things were created through him and for him, and in him all things hold together. He is the head of the church and the firstborn from the dead, and through him God reconciled all things, making peace by the blood of his cross. We sang I'll Fly Away and In the Beginning. The one who made everything is the one who brings us home.
151: Psalm 130 starts at the bottom: out of the depths I cry to you, O Lord. The psalmist knows that if God kept a record of sins, no one could stand. But with God there is forgiveness. So he waits for the Lord more than watchmen wait for the morning, and he tells all of God's people to hope in him, because with the Lord there is steadfast love and plentiful redemption. First Peter 5:10-11 speaks to the same kind of waiting. After you have suffered a little while, the God of all grace will himself restore, confirm, strengthen and establish you. We sang Lord, I Need You and Out of the Depths. Both are prayers for people who cannot fix themselves and know who can.
152: Psalm 23 ends with a promise: goodness and mercy will follow me all the days of my life, and I will dwell in the house of the Lord forever. David is sure about how his story ends. Isaiah 25:8-9 describes that ending. God will swallow up death forever. He will wipe away tears from all faces. And on that day his people will say, this is our God. We have waited for him, and he has saved us. Let us be glad and rejoice in his salvation. We sang Absent From Flesh and Oh to See You. Both look past death to the moment a believer sees Christ. The waiting is real, and it will be worth it.
